EXPLORER 2 · LESSON 6

First Actions & Body Parts for Babies 9–12 Months

Age 9–12 MonthsSubject Talk & ThinkClass Baby 2Duration 3–5 minutes

Between nine and twelve months, babies become little copiers: they wave, clap, point and love it when you name what they are doing. This class uses twelve simple cards — a hand, a foot, eyes, a nose, a mouth, then clapping, waving, eating, drinking, sleeping, pointing and smiling — shown one at a time while you say the word or do the action together.

There is no script and nothing to test. You talk and play, your baby looks and moves, and the words for their little body and everyday actions grow out of real, happy moments. Short sessions of three to five minutes are all it takes.

Start Today’s Class ↓Twelve cards, one at a time. Say the word, do the action — copy-me play wins at this age.

PARENT INSTRUCTIONS

How to use this activity

Sit with your baby when they are awake, comfortable and interested. Show one card at a time and say the word or action naturally. Keep your language short and clear.

For example: ‘Hand.’ ‘These are eyes.’ ‘Clap, clap!’ ‘Wave bye-bye.’ ‘Baby is sleeping.’

When possible, connect the picture to your baby’s own body or to an action you can do together. For example, say ‘hand’ while gently showing your own hand, or clap your hands while saying ‘clap’.

Give your baby time to look, listen, move or respond in their own way. There is no need to test them or expect them to copy every action.

Keep the activity short and stop when your baby loses interest.

Every baby develops differently. Kiddo School age ranges are guides, not tests or developmental deadlines.

TRY TOGETHER

Little things to say.

Prompts for you, not for the cards — say them softly while your baby looks.

  • Where are your hands? Here are your hands.
  • Clap, clap!
  • Wave bye-bye.
  • Point!
  • Smile!
  • Time to sleep.
REAL-WORLD CONNECTION

Practice in Real Life

Continue the lesson naturally during your day.

  • During dressing: “Foot.”
  • During bath time: “Hand.”
  • When someone leaves: “Wave bye-bye.”
  • During play: “Clap, clap!”
  • When baby smiles: “Smile!”

    Hand — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Body words live on the body, and this card starts the Baby 2 habit: name the part where it lives, then let your baby’s own hands answer.

    What is this?

    A hand is the reaching, grabbing, clapping tool at the end of each arm — and at 9–12 months it is the busiest part of your baby’s body. The card shows a single open hand, drawn big and plain, so the word has a picture worth studying.

    What does it mean?

    Between nine and twelve months hands take over: they grab the spoon, rake the crumb, learn the pincer pick and beat a joyful rhythm on everything within reach. Naming the hand gives your baby a word for the instrument doing all that work.

    What does the child need to know?

    The method is touch-and-say: name "hand" while a hand is actually doing something — patting, holding, banging. Body words stick when the part is felt as well as shown, so the card opens the naming and your baby’s own skin finishes it.

    Why this matters

    Body-part words are usually among the earliest vocabulary a baby understands, because they are always available, always touchable and always in use. A named hand also feeds imitation — clapping, waving and pointing all run on hands.

    What it teaches

    Body awareness, vocabulary understanding (words known long before they are said), pincer grip practice, and the imitation loop this whole stage is built on.

    Words to learn

    handfingersopenwidetapclap

    Say this to your child

    “"Hand! This is a hand. See the fingers, all in a row. Here is your hand — hello, hand. And here is my hand. Hands hold, hands tap, hands clap. What busy hands you have."”

    Step by step

    1. Sit your baby on your lap with both their hands in view, then show the card: "Hand. This is a hand."
    2. Press your baby’s palm gently against the card so picture and feeling arrive together — hand, card, hand.
    3. Open and close your own free hand slowly beside it, saying "open... wide..." and let your baby study the moving fingers.
    4. Offer one finger to grip, then name it again: "Hand. You are holding my hand." The grip itself is this card’s live demonstration.
    5. Finish by patting the card together, one palm over the other, and stop while the game is still fun.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a single open hand — big, plain and nothing else on the card. Say exactly that much, then turn to the better show: your baby’s hands, gripping, patting and spreading, the moving version of the same picture.

    Ask your child

    Watch what the hands do once the word has landed: a grab at the card, a pat, fingers spreading against the picture? Wonder aloud, to nobody in particular: "I wonder if that grip counts as applause yet."

    What your child can say or do

    A palm slapping flat onto the card, fingers raking at its edge, a pincer pick at one corner, or both hands meeting in an accidental first clap — at 9–12 months every one of these is the hand card being answered.

    Out in the real world

    Hands fill the day: the hand that holds the spoon, the hand that waves at the window, the hand that finds yours in a dark room. Say the word at each one and the card repeats itself a dozen times before dinner.

    Try it together

    Hand sandwich: your hand, then the card, then your baby’s hand, patting the stack in turns. Simple repetition plus touch — and the giggles it pulls are the sign the game is working.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you say the word while the part was actually being used, and did your baby land one honest grab or pat? A word on a still card is half a lesson; a word on a moving hand is the whole thing.

    Parent tips

    Follow the hands, not the plan: if your baby would rather chew the corner than study the picture, that is a nine-month-old’s honest review. Naming hands during real grips — spoon, rail, your nose — matters more than any second look at the card.

    Staying safe

    Keep the card in your hands, not in an unattended grip: paper edges soften with chewing and can flake. Mouthing is normal learning at this age — inspect the card afterwards, and retire any corner that is turning to pulp.

    This lesson pairs with the Hand flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).

    Foot — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The foot card brings the word down to floor level, where your baby actually lives. This lesson names feet where they work — kicking, stamping, standing — and lets a toe-count be the encore.

    What is this?

    A foot is the body part your baby stands, kicks and cruises on, ten toes included. The card shows a friendly bare foot so the word has a clear picture, and your baby supplies the wriggling originals.

    What does it mean?

    At 9–12 months many babies pull to stand, cruise the furniture and discover that feet are transport. Naming the foot while it kicks or stamps ties the word to the strongest body sensation your baby has — which is exactly why it sticks.

    What does the child need to know?

    Feet come with built-in games: toes to count, soles to tickle, socks to battle off. Borrow the moments that already happen — the nappy change, the bath, the sock fight — and the word collects dozens of honest rehearsals a day.

    Why this matters

    Body words learned on the body become the base of self-awareness: your baby is mapping "me" part by part. The foot also carries early independence — standing, cruising, the first steps — so its name rides along with every milestone.

    What it teaches

    Body mapping, standing and cruising strength, toe awareness, and vocabulary understanding — words known long before they are said.

    Words to learn

    foottoesticklekickstampbare

    Say this to your child

    “"Foot! One little foot. Toes — one, two, three, four, five. Kick, kick, goes the foot. Tickle, tickle, little toes. Where does the foot go? The foot goes everywhere."”

    Step by step

    1. Catch a barefoot moment — after the sock battle or before the bath — and bring the card down to floor level: "Foot. This is a foot."
    2. Touch the card’s foot, then hold your baby’s foot gently: "Foot. Your foot." The word lands where the part lives.
    3. Count the toes out loud with a slow touch each: "One, two, three, four, five toes." You are not teaching numbers; you are making the foot interesting.
    4. Let your baby kick or stamp the card where it lies, and name it as the foot lands: "Foot! Kick."
    5. Finish with one quick toe wiggle-tickle and a last "foot" — ending on a laugh is how this word earns its keep.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork shows a friendly bare foot, drawn simply with nothing else on the card. Name heel and toes as far as the picture plainly offers, then watch the better artwork: the kicking, grabbing feet on your lap.

    Ask your child

    Watch the feet while you name: a kick at the card, toes curling at the touch, a grab for the opposite foot? Wonder aloud: "I wonder whether that kick was a yes."

    What your child can say or do

    A double kick that thumps the card, toes seized proudly in one fist, a foot hoisted up to hand for inspection, or the first wobbly pull-to-stand on your knees — all foot-card answers, and the standing one is a milestone in costume.

    Out in the real world

    Feet work all day: kicking in the bath, stamping on the kitchen floor, escaping their socks at every change. Each bare foot is a replay — one word, "foot", and the card lives again.

    Try it together

    This little piggy, once through, then stop. The slow build and the sudden wiggle at the end is a full comedy show at this age — and it keeps toes interesting long enough for the word foot to ride along.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word land during a real foot moment rather than a drill, and did your baby laugh or kick at least once? Two yeses and the foot card has done its work for the day.

    Parent tips

    The sock fight is not an obstacle — it is the lesson. Naming feet while socks come off beats any table-top session. If your baby spends the week pulling socks off, fine: the foot is the star and the socks are the curtain.

    Staying safe

    Feet on a paper card are fine; the card under standing feet is not — it slides. Keep sessions seated or lying, and keep the card out of the cot, where a busy foot will find it at 3 a.m. for entirely different purposes.

    This lesson pairs with the Foot flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).

    Eyes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Your baby has been reading eyes since the day they were born; this card simply attaches a word to the favourite subject. The lesson is a three-stop naming tour, then quiet watching.

    What is this?

    Eyes are the organs of looking — and at 9–12 months they carry a second job: reading. Your baby checks your eyes to know whether a moment is safe, funny or worth crying about. The card shows a pair of bright eyes and names them.

    What does it mean?

    Naming the eyes works twice. It gives your baby a body word they already love to look at, and it sharpens the social tool they use most — the glance that asks you how a moment is going, and waits for your eyes to answer.

    What does the child need to know?

    Use the three-stop tour: touch the card’s eyes, then your own, then your baby’s, saying the word once at each stop. Three landings in five seconds teach more than ten repetitions in one place — and the third stop is the one that counts.

    Why this matters

    Understanding body words is a language milestone that arrives before speaking does, and eyes are usually among the first understood — they turn up in songs, games and mirror play. The card turns a favourite game into a word.

    What it teaches

    Body-part vocabulary, shared attention (looking where you look), eye contact as conversation, and the visual skills this stage keeps polishing.

    Words to learn

    eyesblinklookpeekbrighthere

    Say this to your child

    “"Eyes! I see you with my eyes. Blink, blink. Here are your eyes — bright and busy. Peek-a-boo, the eyes come back. Eyes look, eyes blink, eyes say hello without a sound."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and touch the pictured eyes: "Eyes. These are eyes."
    2. Move to your own eyes and point: "My eyes. I am looking at you." Hold the gaze a beat — your baby is reading you.
    3. Finish the tour on your baby: touch gently beside their eyes — "Your eyes" — and wait for a blink, a squint or a stare back.
    4. Play one slow blink of your own; many babies this age blink back or laugh, and either reply means the game is working.
    5. Close with a round of peek-a-boo, the card over your face — the eyes reappearing is the joke, and the word rides on the laugh.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a pair of bright eyes and nothing else — a big, clear picture of the exact thing your baby seeks out in every face. After the naming, let your baby’s eyes be the exhibit: where do they look when you look away?

    Ask your child

    Watch the three stops: does the gaze follow your finger from card to your face? Does the slow blink pull a reply? Wonder aloud: "I wonder how long you have known which part is which."

    What your child can say or do

    Eyes that track your pointing finger, a blink offered back, a stare that holds on your face instead of the card, or a crow of delight at the peek-a-boo reveal — answering with looks rather than words is exactly how this age talks.

    Out in the real world

    Eyes run through the whole day: yours over the cot rail, a sibling making faces, the mirror at bath time. Each glance is a chance for the word — said once, softly, at the moment the eyes meet.

    Try it together

    Mirror glance: hold your baby at a mirror, point at the four eyes in the glass, then at the real ones. Doubles and originals — your baby will not sort them out for months, but the staring contest it starts is glorious.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you complete all three stops of the naming tour, and did your baby answer at least one look with a look? The exchange — not the pointing — is the true lesson of this card.

    Parent tips

    Do not chase the word with repetition; three landings, then quiet. If your baby is more interested in grabbing the card than studying it, let the grab happen on your terms and keep naming. Interest in eyes never needs manufacturing at this age — only naming.

    Staying safe

    Keep tour fingers on brows and cheeks, away from the eyes themselves. Hold the card firmly during blink games — a snatched edge can flick — and hand it back to your own hand after each round.

    This lesson pairs with the Eyes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).

    Nose — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The nose card is the set’s comedian: short, silly and endlessly repeatable. This lesson runs the boop ritual that makes the word unforgettable — and keeps it gentle enough to stay funny.

    What is this?

    A nose is the breathing, smelling, boopable bump in the middle of the face. The card shows a small round nose; your face and your baby’s supply the other two, and the boop — a feather-light fingertip tap — supplies the fun.

    What does it mean?

    Babies remember words that arrive with a feeling, and the nose boop pairs a word with a touch, a surprise and usually a laugh. That three-for-one deal is why nose so often ends up among the first body words a baby truly knows.

    What does the child need to know?

    Keep the boop light and the ritual identical every time: card, you, baby, the word at each stop. Predictability is the joke — many babies start grinning before the third boop lands, which tells you the sequence has been learned.

    Why this matters

    Ritual games do more than teach one word: they teach that interactions have a shape, that the shape repeats, and that your baby can predict and enjoy it. That expectation is the foundation humour, language and turn-taking all stand on.

    What it teaches

    Body-part vocabulary, tactile awareness, anticipation and prediction, and turn-taking — boop, giggle, boop again.

    Words to learn

    noseboopsniffroundgentleagain

    Say this to your child

    “"Nose! Boop — a nose on the card. Boop — my nose. Boop — your nose. One little round nose, sniff sniff. Everybody has a nose, and yours goes boop the best."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and land the first boop on the picture: "Nose. Boop!"
    2. Boop your own nose: "My nose. Boop!" Exaggerate the word, never the poke.
    3. End the tour with the softest tap on your baby’s nose: "Your nose. Boop." Then stop and watch.
    4. If a grin arrives, run the round again in the same order — card, you, baby — because the pattern is as much the lesson as the word.
    5. Finish with a sniff towards the card: "Nose!" Some babies copy the sniff with their whole face; that is a bonus act, not the goal.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a small round nose, drawn plain and friendly with nothing busy around it — say that much and no more. The rest of the show is touch: three real noses, one word, and whatever the third boop shakes loose.

    Ask your child

    Watch the third stop: does the grin arrive before your finger lands — prediction — or after — surprise? Wonder aloud: "I wonder when you started knowing what comes next."

    What your child can say or do

    A giggle starting before the third boop, a hand rising to boop your nose in return, a whole-face sniff attempt, or a leaning-in that clearly asks for another round — all of it is the nose card working exactly as designed.

    Out in the real world

    Noses are everywhere and always attached to someone worth booping: the mirror, a sibling, a grandparent on a video call — boop the screen, gently. One word covers every face in the family.

    Try it together

    Reverse boop: take your baby’s hand and help it boop your nose, then their own. Guided first, independent later — the hand-over-hand version is how this game becomes theirs.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the ritual stay identical — same order, same feather touch — and did your baby laugh or try a boop back? If the word nose now pulls a grin all by itself, the card has landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep boops feather-light and stop while it is still funny; a nose game that runs long stops being a game. If your baby is snuffly or tired, skip the touch and simply point at the three noses — the word still lands.

    Staying safe

    Boop the tip of the nose only, never inside the nostrils, and check your own fingernails before face games. If your baby pulls the card towards their face, take it back — a paper corner near an eye is the one real risk here.

    This lesson pairs with the Nose flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).

    Mouth — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The mouth card names your baby’s headquarters: food goes in, sounds come out, and everything interesting happens in between. This lesson names it during the things the mouth already does all day.

    What is this?

    A mouth is the opening your baby eats, babbles and blows raspberries with — at 9–12 months possibly the hardest-working part of the whole body. The card shows a simple, friendly mouth and gives the busy thing a name.

    What does it mean?

    Babies this age watch mouths intently — it is how they study how sounds are made. Naming the mouth while it works hands that intense watching a word, and the word a hundred natural rehearsals between breakfast and bath.

    What does the child need to know?

    Slow open-and-close is the demonstration that hooks attention: open your mouth wide, close it, then say "mouth". Your baby is old enough to study the movement and young enough to find it gripping — three rounds, then stop.

    Why this matters

    Mouth-watching feeds straight into speech: babies copy the shapes they see before they manage the sounds they hear. A named mouth also links forward to eating words — it is where every eating word eventually lands.

    What it teaches

    Speech preparation through mouth-watching, body-part vocabulary, oral-motor practice (babbling, raspberry-blowing), and early imitation of facial movement.

    Words to learn

    mouthopencloseyumblowkiss

    Say this to your child

    “"Mouth! Here is a mouth. My mouth opens wide — ahh — and closes. Your mouth babbles: mamama, bababa. The mouth says yum at dinner, and the mouth blows kisses. What a busy little mouth."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and name it: "Mouth. This is a mouth."
    2. Open and close your own mouth slowly and silently, three times, then say "mouth" — the pause lets your baby connect the moving lips with the word.
    3. Touch your baby’s mouth area lightly with the back of your hand and say it once more: "Your mouth."
    4. Blow a gentle raspberry and name it: "Mouth! The mouth goes pbbbt." Silly sounds are mouth advertising, and this age buys it every time.
    5. If a babble comes back, answer it warmly — your baby is using their mouth to talk to you, which is the whole point of the card.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a simple, friendly mouth — plainly drawn, nothing else on the card. Name it and move on quickly, because the interesting mouth in the room is the one currently babbling at you; that one is the live version.

    Ask your child

    Watch during the slow open-and-close: does your baby’s own mouth move along, or do the eyes lock onto your lips? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which shape you are saving up for later."

    What your child can say or do

    A babble burst aimed at you, lips opening and closing in copycat slow motion, a raspberry returned with interest, or a mouth already opening at the word "yum" — the mouth answering about the mouth is this card at its best.

    Out in the real world

    The mouth performs all day: yawning at wake-up, humming through dinner, blowing bubbles in the bath. Name it at one or two of those moments and the card has been shown a dozen times without ever being picked up.

    Try it together

    Copy-cat mouths: slow open, slow close, tiny "o", big grin — hold each shape for two seconds. You are not drilling; you are showing that faces make moves, and moves can be answered.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you hold the slow mouth-watching long enough for your baby to study it, and did a babble or a copy land in the quiet afterwards? The stillness between moves is where the learning happens.

    Parent tips

    Narrate, do not demand: no "say mama" pressure — the word today is mouth, and the babbling is your baby’s own business. If mealtimes are calmer than playtimes, run the card then; mouths are most watchable when they are working.

    Staying safe

    Keep fingers and card away from the mouth itself — hands washed, card edges inspected — because at this age everything arrives there eventually anyway. Chewing the corner is data, not misbehaviour; pulped corners go in the bin.

    This lesson pairs with the Mouth flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).

    Clapping — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    From here the set turns from body parts to actions, and clapping leads the way: the card holds the move still, and your baby gets to set it going. This lesson paces the imitation so the first clap has room to arrive.

    What is this?

    Clapping is two hands meeting in a slap of celebration — and at 9–12 months it is the imitation trick of the age: show the move, wait, and many babies join within days or weeks. The card shows two hands mid-clap and names the action.

    What does it mean?

    A first clap is not just cute; it is proof of imitation — your baby saw a movement, kept it in mind and produced it back. That copy-me circuit is the engine of everything this stage teaches, and clapping is usually where it first shows.

    What does the child need to know?

    Model slowly and loudly enough to notice: clap, pause, clap, pause. Then one guided clap, your hands closing softly over your baby’s, then open space and silence — the wait after the model is where self-made claps are born. Do not fill it.

    Why this matters

    Imitation is how babies download culture: waving, spoon use, finger foods, eventually every game and every word. The first clap is the first time the copy-me circuit visibly completes, which is why the whole room cheers when it does.

    What it teaches

    Motor imitation (the milestone beneath the milestone), two-handed coordination, rhythm and timing, and social celebration — clapping as shared joy, not just noise.

    Words to learn

    claphandspatbangmorehooray

    Say this to your child

    “"Clapping! Clap, clap, clap. Hands come together — clap! Pat, pat, pat goes the baby. Clap for the ball, clap for the dog, clap for you. Hooray! Clapping says hooray without a word."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say the word in rhythm: "Clapping! Clap, clap." Tap the two pictured hands as you say it.
    2. Model two slow claps with a full pause between — slow enough that the hands coming together can actually be watched.
    3. Take your baby’s hands and make one gentle clap together, then let go and stay quiet for five whole seconds.
    4. If no clap comes, model once more and let the silence stand; if a clap comes — self-made, sloppy, magnificent — cheer like it is news, because it is.
    5. End by clapping about something real: "Clap for the cup! Clap for you!" Actions need occasions, and this age has them everywhere.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork shows a pair of hands clapping, frozen at the moment of contact — big and clear. Say that, then produce the live version an arm’s length away; the card shows the move, your hands prove it repeats.

    Ask your child

    Watch the wait after your model: do the hands drift towards each other, pat the card, bang the tray instead? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which part of that you are practising in there."

    What your child can say or do

    One self-made clap after days of watching, both hands beating a joyful rhythm on the high-chair tray, hands patted part-way together and closing in over the week, or a first clap delivered right on "hooray" — all of it is imitation coming online.

    Out in the real world

    Clapping fills the week: applause at the park, a song with actions, a "yay" after a mighty sneeze. Wherever hands meet, one word — "clap!" — turns the moment into a replay of this card.

    Try it together

    Clap-and-wait is the whole game: you clap twice, stop, and look expectant. The expectant face after the pause is the invitation; skip it and your baby stays an audience instead of becoming a performer.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you leave a real silence after modelling — five seconds, no prompting — and did you celebrate any attempt, however partial? The wait is your half of the skill; the attempt is theirs.

    Parent tips

    Resist hand-over-hand marathons: one guided clap per session is plenty, because the goal is a self-started move, not a puppet show. Bang-on-tray days count too — name the banging, and the clapping arrives when the hands agree.

    Staying safe

    Clap facing your baby, away from table edges and hard corners — enthusiastic slapping and furniture negotiate badly. Keep the guided clap gentle; small wrists prefer applause to force.

    This lesson pairs with the Clapping flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).

    Waving — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Waving is the gesture your baby is most likely to perform for an audience, and doorways hand out free lessons all day. This card catches the movement mid-wave and gives it a word.

    What is this?

    Waving is a hand moving hello or goodbye — usually the first social gesture a baby performs on request. The card shows a hand mid-wave; the real performances happen at doors, windows, mirrors and every departing relative.

    What does it mean?

    A wave is communication without words: your baby sees someone go, moves a hand, and the someone answers. Naming it gives the gesture a soundtrack, and the daily traffic of arrivals and departures gives it honest stages all week.

    What does the child need to know?

    Wave about real goodbyes, not at the card: the front door, the window, the sibling leaving for school. Gestures live inside routines — the more real exits the word attaches to, the sooner your baby connects the movement with its meaning.

    Why this matters

    Gestures come before words and predict them: babies who wave and point early are building the turn-taking system that speech runs on. A wave on request is also your baby’s first deliberate social act — a small hand with a large milestone in it.

    What it teaches

    Gestural communication, social routines (hello and goodbye), imitation of movement, and the understanding that actions can be called up by words.

    Words to learn

    wavebyehellohandoutagain

    Say this to your child

    “"Waving! Wave bye-bye. The hand goes out and back — out and back. Bye-bye, Daddy. Bye-bye, window. Hello, morning! Waving says hello and waving says goodbye, and your little hand knows both."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and move it gently side to side: "Waving! Wave bye-bye." The moving card demonstrates before you do.
    2. Wave your own hand slowly at the card: "Wave, wave." Exaggerate the turn at the wrist so the movement can be studied.
    3. Take your baby’s hand and wave it once towards the card or a real window, then release and watch what comes back.
    4. Stage one real goodbye — a leaving parent, a sibling, a mirror — and run the word there: "Bye-bye! Wave!" Real audiences make real waves.
    5. Finish by waving hello and goodbye at your baby yourself, and answer any wave back with a warm "hello!" — the reply is what makes the gesture worth repeating.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a single hand caught mid-wave — fingers up, the movement implied. Say that much, then look at the hands in the room: the card freezes the wave, and your baby’s hand is the one that animates it.

    Ask your child

    Watch the doorway moments across the week: does an arm lift when the word lands, or does the wave arrive late and unasked? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which goodbye is your favourite."

    What your child can say or do

    An arm pumped up and down at the closed door after someone leaves, a wrist-only wave aimed at the window, waving at the mirror with total delight, or the gesture offered at random — at 9–12 months, off-schedule waving is rehearsal, not confusion.

    Out in the real world

    Waves run through every day: the postwoman, the neighbour’s dog, a grandparent on a video call, the bath toy going "bye-bye" down the plughole. Every goodbye is a stage, and the word is the ticket.

    Try it together

    Wave relay: you wave, wait, and answer any wave back with another wave. Long chains of hello-and-back are exactly what conversation feels like to a baby — the wave is simply the first thing they can say in it.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you attach the word to at least one real goodbye this week, and did you answer every wave you caught? A wave ignored is a letter unanswered, and babies notice.

    Parent tips

    Do not drill the wave at the card alone — gestures grow on people and doors, not on paper. If your baby waved wildly for a week then stopped, that is normal calibration; keep waving, and the pause passes.

    Staying safe

    Wave with arms in open space, away from door frames and table edges, and keep the card out of your baby’s hand during the excited part — a paper edge flaps worse than it waves. Doorway goodbyes need one grown-up per doorway.

    This lesson pairs with the Waving flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST ACTIONS & BODY PARTS · AGES 9–12 MONTHS

    Eating — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    No card in the set gets more live performances: eating happens on schedule, with an audience and props. This lesson shows how to name the action mid-meal so the word lands where the food does.

    What is this?

    Eating is taking food in — spoon in the card’s picture, finger foods in your baby’s fist. At 9–12 months your baby is deep in the self-feeding project: mashed everything, pincer picks and a spoon held with more hope than aim. The card names the thing they are already experts in.

    What does it mean?

    Action words are the shy ones of early vocabulary — harder to point at than nouns — but meal routines give eating a stage no other verb gets: a beginning, a middle, an end and a bib. Naming it mid-bite gives a verb its clearest chance.

    What does the child need to know?

    Say the word while the mouth is busy: "Eating! You are eating." Timing is the whole trick — before the bite is a forecast, during is the word, after is a review. Aim for during, once or twice a meal, and let the meal stay a meal.

    Why this matters

    Verbs open the door to sentences: eating, drinking, sleeping give your baby a grammar of daily life long before they can say any of it. Understanding "eating" also lets your baby predict — the word itself begins to mean food is coming.

    What it teaches

    Verb vocabulary through routine, understanding ahead of speaking, self-feeding skills (pincer grip, spoon practice), and shared attention at meals.

    Words to learn

    eatingbiteyumspoonmoreall gone

    Say this to your child

    “"Eating! The baby on the card is eating, spoon going in. You are eating too — yum, yum. Bite by bite, in it goes. Spoon up, mouth open. All gone! Eating is what we do, three times a day."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card just before a meal, not in the middle of the chaos: "Eating! The baby is eating, just like you."
    2. Let your baby hold the card and bang it gently on the tray — the card is about them, and they should treat it accordingly.
    3. At the next meal, name it once mid-bite: "Eating. Yum." Then carry on; the meal is the main event and the word is the garnish.
    4. Point at the card’s spoon, then the real spoon: "Spoon. You have a spoon too." Matching picture to prop is the game this age plays best.
    5. Finish the meal with "all gone!" and both hands turned over — the ending of eating is as nameable as the middle, and babies love a formal finish.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork shows a baby at a meal, spoon going in — a scene rather than a single object, so there is plenty to name honestly: the spoon, the open mouth, the business of it. Then look up: the same scene, starring your baby.

    Ask your child

    Watch the mid-bite naming: do the eyes flick to you, does the mouth open wider, does the hand pause? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you knew that was the word for this."

    What your child can say or do

    A pincer pick of a puff delivered straight to the mouth, the mouth opening before the spoon arrives, the spoon banged like a drumstick between bites, or a pause and a look at the word "eating" — understanding running ahead of speech is exactly what this age does.

    Out in the real world

    Every meal is the card: breakfast, lunch, dinner, snacks, the biscuit at grandma’s. Name the action at one or two of them and the vocabulary of daily life starts assembling itself.

    Try it together

    Feed the card: pretend to spoon-feed the picture — "in it goes, yum!" — then offer your baby the spoon for one real bite. Prop play makes the routine funny, and funny gets remembered.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word land mid-action at least once today, and did the meal stay calm afterwards? Narration is seasoning; the meal itself is still the meal.

    Parent tips

    One or two namings per meal is the ceiling — a running commentary turns dinner into a lesson, and nobody eats well in a classroom. If your baby is too busy eating to look at you, fine: the word was heard by the part that was listening.

    Staying safe

    Sit upright for every bite, keep foods soft and cut small for this stage, and stay within arm’s reach through the meal — gagging is loud, but choking is silent, and silence is the reason a grown-up stays close. Cards wait until the tray is for playing, not for lunch.

    This lesson pairs with the Eating flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST ACTIONS & BODY PARTS · AGES 9–12 MONTHS

    Drinking — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Drinking is eating’s quieter sibling: on schedule, all day, and full of new skill at this age as open cups and beakers enter the picture. This card names the routine your baby is currently mastering.

    What is this?

    Drinking is taking liquid in — from cup, beaker or straw. The card shows a baby at a cup, mid-sip; your baby is learning the two-handed hold, the tip, and the inevitable soak. The word arrives exactly when the skill does.

    What does it mean?

    Drinking is one of the first actions your baby both performs and controls: nobody can drink for them. Naming it hands over a word for something they own, and pairs it with eating as the start of a verb collection for daily life.

    What does the child need to know?

    Name it at the sip: "Drinking. Sip, sip." Then name your own — "Mummy is drinking too" — the same word for a bigger cup. The two-version naming teaches that one word covers many drinkers, which is how vocabulary scales.

    Why this matters

    Cup drinking at 9–12 months is a real developmental project: hand-to-mouth coordination, tipping, swallowing control. A word for the project marks progress and lets your baby recognise the routine in language before they can request it.

    What it teaches

    Two-handed grip and tip control, hand-to-mouth coordination, routine vocabulary, and the pairing of thing (cup) with action (drinking) that later grammar stands on.

    Words to learn

    drinksipcupgulpthirstyahh

    Say this to your child

    “"Drinking! Sip, sip, sip goes the baby. Up comes the cup, down goes the drink. I am drinking too — ahh! Two hands on the cup, just like a big one. All gone! Drinking is thirsty work."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at a calm drink moment — after the first sip, while hands are briefly free: "Drinking! The baby is drinking."
    2. Hold the card next to your baby’s real cup: same word, two pictures. "Cup. Drinking."
    3. At the next sip, say it quietly mid-drink: "Drinking. Sip, sip." No fanfare; the routine is doing the teaching.
    4. Take a loud, obvious sip of your own drink and narrate it: "I am drinking too. Ahh." Exaggeration is welcome here.
    5. Finish with the empty cup: "All gone!" — the end of drinking is its own scene, and naming it teaches sequence.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork shows a baby mid-drink, cup held steady and plainly drawn. Name the action and the cup, then compare with the live version on the tray — the card is the portrait, your baby the performance.

    Ask your child

    Watch the cup-handling across the week: is the two-handed hold steadier today than on Monday, does the tip arrive earlier? Wonder aloud: "I wonder how long until you drink without wearing any."

    What your child can say or do

    Both hands wrapping the cup and lifting it alone, a tip that finally works, sips offered and then refused with a turned head — refusing is communicating too — or a satisfied "ahh" after a long gulp: every one is the drinking card, lived.

    Out in the real world

    Drinks mark the day: morning milk, water after the park, the beaker at lunch. Each one is a replay — one soft word at one real sip keeps the card running between lessons.

    Try it together

    Cheers! Tap your cup gently against your baby’s, then both drink. The toast makes drinking a two-person game, and the clink is an accident of joy this age finds hilarious.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you name both the baby’s drink and your own with the same word, and did the naming stay under three mentions? Restraint keeps routines restful and words welcome.

    Parent tips

    Spills are tuition fees, not failures — name the drinking, wipe the water, move on. If your baby prefers to dunk the card rather than study it, retrieve and dry; this card was always going to meet the cup eventually.

    Staying safe

    Stay within arm’s reach for every drink at this age; tipping cups and lying backs disagree. Keep sips upright and skip drinks in the cot altogether — upright drinking is the safe kind. Choose cups small hands can actually grip.

    This lesson pairs with the Drinking flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST ACTIONS & BODY PARTS · AGES 9–12 MONTHS

    Sleeping — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Every set needs a quiet card, and this is it: a baby asleep, a hush built in. Shown at the same point each day, it becomes less a lesson and more a cue — which is the lesson.

    What is this?

    Sleeping is the resting state your baby visits several times a day and contests fiercely at bedtime. The card shows a baby fast asleep, eyes shut; the word, said softly at the right moment, becomes part of the wind-down itself.

    What does it mean?

    Babies learn words from the texture around them as much as from the sound: a word said in a lowered voice, at the same point of the same routine, gets a special tag — predictable, safe, sleepy. That tag is why routine words stick so well.

    What does the child need to know?

    The trick is the voice: show the card and drop to a near-whisper — "Shhh. The baby is sleeping." Babies read a dropped voice instantly, and many soften with it. The card is a cue for you as much as for them.

    Why this matters

    Understanding "sleeping" helps your baby predict what comes next, and prediction is comfort: the card before the nap becomes the signal that sleep is safe and coming. A named nap-time routine gives the day a shape your baby can trust.

    What it teaches

    Routine and sequence understanding, word learning through tone and context, self-settling cues, and the first ideas that actions end and begin — awake, sleeping, awake.

    Words to learn

    sleepingshhhsleepynight-nightrestquiet

    Say this to your child

    “"Shhh — sleeping. The baby on the card is sleeping. Eyes closed, all quiet. You are sleepy too, little one. Night-night, sleeping baby. We will say hello when you wake up."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at the start of the wind-down, your voice already low: "Shhh. Sleeping. The baby is sleeping."
    2. Point at the closed eyes on the card, then close your own — the comparison teaches without another word.
    3. Say one sentence about the routine, quietly: "You are sleepy too. Soon it is your turn."
    4. Put the card away together before the nap, with a whispered "bye-bye, sleeping baby" — endings are part of the ritual.
    5. On waking, reopen the story brightly: "You woke up! Hello!" The contrast between sleeping and awake is the day’s real vocabulary lesson.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork shows a baby asleep — closed eyes, soft lines, the quietest picture in the set. Describe it in a whisper and let the hush do the rest; this card’s job is to lower the temperature of the room.

    Ask your child

    Watch the wind-down across a week: does the low voice alone start the softening before the card even appears? Wonder aloud, very quietly: "I wonder when the whisper became the signal."

    What your child can say or do

    A body that settles as your voice drops, eyes closing mid-look at the card, a rub of their own eyes at the word "sleepy", or — the honest version — an arch and a protest, because some days the cue simply arrives too early.

    Out in the real world

    Sleeping happens all around your baby: a sibling napping, a dog asleep on the rug, the pram at the park, dark rooms after lunch. Each quiet scene is a chance for one whispered "sleeping" — the softest replay in the set.

    Try it together

    Bedtime for teddy: tuck a bear under a cloth, whisper "shhh, sleeping", and pat it gently. Pretend sleep is the rehearsal of the real thing — and this age takes teddy care extremely seriously.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the card appear at the same point of the routine several days running, and did you manage the whisper? Consistency, not repetition, is what turns this card into a cue.

    Parent tips

    Run this card as a ritual, never as a lesson — rituals hate being rehearsed. If naps are falling apart this week, shelve the card; sleep regression and flashcards should not meet. The word keeps, and the routine comes back.

    Staying safe

    Cards stay out of the cot — sleep surfaces hold nothing soft, loose or papery, full stop. Wind-down happens in your lap or on the floor, and the card goes away with you before sleep begins.

    This lesson pairs with the Sleeping flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST ACTIONS & BODY PARTS · AGES 9–12 MONTHS

    Pointing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    A pointing finger is on its way to being your baby’s superpower — the first way to ask, request and share a discovery without speech. This card catches the gesture mid-point and teaches you the response that makes it flourish.

    What is this?

    Pointing is extending one finger towards something — to ask, to show, to wonder. Around this age the first true points appear: index finger out, arm up, aimed. The card shows a single hand, index finger out and aiming; your baby is about to supply the living version.

    What does it mean?

    A point is a question with no words: that, there, more. It is the start of joint attention — two people attending to one thing on purpose — and one of the most important milestones of the first year. The card names the gesture; your answers give it power.

    What does the child need to know?

    The rule that runs the game: when your baby points, name what they point at, instantly and warmly. Not "yes, that" — the actual word: "Dog!" The answer teaches your baby that pointing works, and what keeps the finger coming back.

    Why this matters

    Pointing predicts language: it is the toddler’s first sentence, a gesture with a subject and a question mark. Every answered point feeds vocabulary, shared attention and the deep idea that other people can be asked for information.

    What it teaches

    Joint attention, pointing to request and to share, vocabulary through naming, and the turn-taking loop — point, name, look back, smile.

    Words to learn

    pointtherelookthatmoreyes

    Say this to your child

    “"Pointing! One finger out — there! I point at the card, I point at the light, I point at you. Point at anything and I will name it: dog, cup, ball, moon. A little finger is a way of asking."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and trace the pointing finger with your own: "Pointing! You point at things."
    2. Point at the card itself, then at an object far across the room, naming each: "Card... lamp!" Show that a point travels.
    3. Point at something your baby loves — the window, the family pet — and look back at your baby’s face to check they followed. That look-back is half the skill; you are modelling it.
    4. Wait quietly through the day for your baby’s points, and answer each one with the word for what they mean: "Cup! Yes, your cup."
    5. End the session by pointing at the card’s hand, then your baby’s hand — "Your pointer!" — and letting them take the last turn.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a single hand, one finger extended and aiming — a clean, plain gesture. Say that, then watch the live theatre: the wobbly aim, the check-back eyes. The card drew the arrow; your baby fires it.

    Ask your child

    Watch the points across the day: does the finger come with a sound, a look back at you, a wait for your word? Wonder aloud: "I wonder what you will point at first thing tomorrow."

    What your child can say or do

    A first true index-finger point at something wanted, a whole-hand sweep towards the window that is practising to become a point, pointing at the card and then at you, or a point plus "eh!" — the sound is the caption; the aim is the sentence.

    Out in the real world

    Pointing runs through everything now: the biscuit tin on the shelf, the bird on the fence, the sibling who definitely did it. Your job is not to make points happen — it is to be the dictionary they land in, every time.

    Try it together

    Point-and-name tour: carry your baby towards something they point at and name it up close — "Tap! It is the tap." Following the finger to its target teaches that points lead somewhere, which is what keeps them coming.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you answer every point today with the real word, and did you look back at your baby’s face while pointing yourself? The loop — point, name, check — is the whole technology.

    Parent tips

    Points that want and points that share look the same and both deserve answers; do not bother sorting them yet. If your baby is not pointing yet, keep modelling and answer reaching hands the same way — the finger inherits the habit.

    Staying safe

    The pointing finger pokes — keep it away from eyes, yours included, and keep a firm hold on the card during excited tours. Otherwise this is the gentlest card in the set, which the finger will resent.

    This lesson pairs with the Pointing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST ACTIONS & BODY PARTS · AGES 9–12 MONTHS

    Smiling — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The set ends on the one card your baby has been performing since week six: the smile. This lesson uses it to close card time the way all good routines close — warmly, and on purpose.

    What is this?

    Smiling is happiness arriving on the face — an action and a feeling at once. The card shows a big happy smile; your baby, at 9–12 months, owns a whole repertoire: the grin for games, the shy face for strangers, the beam that greets a parent.

    What does it mean?

    By this age smiles are fully social tools: your baby smiles to greet, to charm, to ask for more of a good game. Naming the smile — "What a smile!" — hands a word to the feeling, and feeling-words are the start of a lifelong conversation.

    What does the child need to know?

    Mirror it and name it: when the smile arrives, make the same one back and say the word. The mirroring tells your baby the expression was received; the word gives the expression a handle. Both halves together make the lesson.

    Why this matters

    Ending a card session with a smile on every face is not a gimmick — warm finishes are what make tomorrow easy. Babies remember how sessions felt, and a smiling close is the best advertisement for doing it all again.

    What it teaches

    Emotional vocabulary, social smiling with intent, mirroring and imitation, and the shared-joy loop that keeps every learning session coming back.

    Words to learn

    smilehappygrinhellobrightagain

    Say this to your child

    “"Smiling! What a big, happy smile. Here is the card’s smile — and here is mine. And there is yours, the best one of all. Smiles say hello, smiles say I love this game, smiles say again, please."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card with a smile already on your face: "Smiling! What a lovely smile."
    2. Point at the card’s smile, then make the same smile yourself, big and held: card, face, card, face.
    3. Wait for your baby’s reply — a grin, a scrunch, a full beam — and name it the moment it lands: "Smile! There it is."
    4. Try the smile in a mirror together if one is near: four smiles in one glass, and your baby will study the doubling happily.
    5. Close the whole set here: put the cards away smiling, say "all done, smile!", and let the good feeling be the last thing the session says.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a big happy smile, wide and friendly, nothing else needed on the card. Say that, then turn to the better exhibit: the live smiles on your lap, arriving for games, greetings and — if you are lucky — the card itself.

    Ask your child

    Watch what pulls the smiles this week: a game, a face, a returning parent? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you are smiling at the smile or at me." Both, probably; both is fine.

    What your child can say or do

    A full open-mouth beam at the card, the shy tuck-in smile for strangers that proves sorting has started, a smile offered and held while waiting for yours back, or a giggle-smile at the mirror — each one is social work, not just sunshine.

    Out in the real world

    Smiles run the whole day: the one that greets a sibling, the one that charms the checkout assistant, the one that ends a crying fit. Each is a replay — one word, "smile!", and the card lives again.

    Try it together

    Smile tennis: make a smile, wait, answer the one that comes back, wait again. Long chains are the point — your baby is learning that faces answer faces, which is the game everyone plays for life.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you mirror and name at least one smile today, and did card time end warmly rather than in a wriggle-away? The finish you keep is the invitation for tomorrow.

    Parent tips

    Smiles cannot be commanded, only invited — drop the eager face and simply wear one. If the day was hard and nobody smiled much, fine: the set starts again tomorrow, and it opens with a hand and ends with a smile.

    Staying safe

    Nothing about smiling needs guarding except the session itself: stop before tiredness turns grumpy, keep the card out of grab-and-gum range, and let the last minute be gentle — happy endings are the safest endings.

    This lesson pairs with the Smiling flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Actions & Body Parts (Baby 2).
